# HANDOFF — take over Katalyst and carry it to a working prototype

You are a fresh agent. You have no memory of how this project got here. This file gives you everything you need to continue. Read it fully, then read `STATUS.md` (newest entry on top), then **`PLAN.md`**.

> **2026-09-21 — the road changed; this file's §2 and §9 describe the project before it did.** Two independent reviews were digested that day. They found three real defects in the engine's arithmetic on the demo map, and that the trade the brief ends in has no code. The road is now: finish stack 04 → **05 sound numbers, then settled shapes** → **06 the trade** → **07 a map you can argue with**. Read **`PLAN.md`** (what, in what order, the definition of done), **`design-after-midpoint-review.md`** (why), and **`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`** (what waits on Kent — nothing in stacks 05–07 is built until he answers). §4–§8 below — how Kent works, git, the environment, worktrees, the lessons — are unchanged and binding. Two working rules are new: **every whole suite, browser run and repeat bar goes through `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`, one at a time**; and **only Hormuz is recorded until Kent explicitly approves more.**

---

## 1. The mission

Build **Katalyst**: a take-home prototype for Catalyst (catalyst.app), a seed-stage company that turns a trading idea stated in plain English into live execution.

**What the tool does, in one sentence:** you type an event you think will happen; Katalyst shows what it would cause, step by step, ending in trades — and lets you change any step to see how the trades change.

The brief is `ASSIGNMENT.md`. The owner is **Kent Gang**, a solo developer. He cares most about four things, in his words: well structured with Docker and tests; proper code design; rigorously documented decisions; and a beautiful, elegant, delightful interface.

**"Done" means:** a reviewer clones the repo, runs one command, and walks the full flow on all four example events from the brief — type a hypothesis, watch the cause-and-effect map draw itself, change a step, compare the two versions, and end on a thesis card with a derived stop-loss. Tests pass with no API key. Every number on screen can show why. Full checklist: `roadmap-03-to-06.md`, "Definition of done" (the boxes stack 03 ticked are ticked).

---

## 2. What is built, as of 2026-09-17 (end of stack 03)

Stacks 01 (skeleton), 02 (schema), **03a (engine) and 03b (canvas)** are merged to `main`. Every pull request up to #27 is squash-merged (a few numbers were never used), and `main` is green on five checks.

**The one sentence to hold on to:** *the engine computes everything and the canvas draws everything, and they have not met.* The canvas reads the stored example and shows every computed number as an absence with a reason ("no engine yet"). Joining them is the first code of stack 04.

**Documents.** `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md`; `ARCHITECTURE.md` (every section says *built* or *planned*); fourteen decision records in `docs/adr/`, **0001–0014, all accepted** — next is **0015**. The spec is a book: `spec/graph/` (4 chapters), `spec/multiverse/` (4: `interventions`, `branches-and-worlds`, `propagation`, `diff`), `spec/workbench/` (6: `color-motion-type`, `tiles-ports-wires`, `layout-and-zoom`, `keyboard-and-access`, `diff-view`, `inspector`, plus the landing page's **worked example cast** and **twelve-line visual review checklist**), and `spec/vocabulary.md` with its **Interface words** table and **Words for a number that is not there**. `spec/generation/` and `spec/thesis/` are landing pages only.

**The server** — `backend/src/katalyst/`:

- `domain/` — the pure core, twelve files, 100% covered, `mypy --strict` clean. Models (`belief`, `proposition`, `link`, `graph`, `intervention`, `branch`, `ids`), `validity.py` (`validate` returns every fault at once; **nineteen codes**: fourteen map faults, four refused edits, one refused comparison), **`patch.py`** (`Assignment`, `apply`, `flatten`, `affected_set`, `introduced_by`), **`propagation.py`** (`World`, `Retraction`, `SeriesState`, `propagate`, `versions_of` — two thousand versions of the map × eight worlds; a supposition is a hard fact until undermined; two seed streams derived per claim), **`diff.py`** (`diff`, `DeltaRow`, `sensitivity` — `shifted` read off the paired difference; rank = size of move × weakest arrow on the best-backed route).
- `engine/` — `ids.py` (the only place an identifier is made) and `worlds.py` (the only place that knows a store or a date). Nothing has ever called a model.
- `fixtures/hormuz.py` — the worked example, now **curated**: two inputs tuned and marked **Tuned**, and every `beliefs.model` equal to its `prior` ("nothing computed yet"). Branch `br_hormuz_then_strike`.
- `api/` — `GET /api/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/about`, `/fixtures`, `/fixtures/{id}`, and **`POST /api/worlds`, `/api/worlds/diff`, `/api/worlds/conditional`** (a refused branch is a 422 carrying every violation). Try: `curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/api/worlds -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"base_id":"hormuz","seed":20261001}'`.
- `grounding/` — an empty package (stack 05).

**The browser app** — `frontend/src/`: `api/schema.ts` (generated, never hand-edited) and `api/client.ts`; `world/` (the `WorldSource` seam, `FixtureWorldSource` live, **`ApiWorldSource` a stub waiting for stack 04**, hand-written `WorldView`, `branchReducer`); `graph/` (canvas, ELK layout on a background thread with pinning, `wires/` with routing and one-pass plate placement, `diff/` with the four structural states); `components/` (Tile, BeliefChip, OriginMark, Inspector, PathBar, DeltaRail, BranchPanel, Outline, CommandPalette, ShortcutsSheet, Launchpad, DirectionReadout); `keyboard/`, `a11y/`; `styles/tokens.css` (the whole visual vocabulary); `e2e/hormuz.spec.ts`.

**Tests: 259 on the server, 177 in the browser (one skipped on purpose — it waits for the join), one keyboard-only end-to-end test.** Continuous integration: `backend`, `frontend`, `types-fresh`, `docker`, `e2e` — **no API key in any of them**.

**What the engine says about Hormuz** (seed 20261001): *"Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck" moves [the Polymarket Brent contract] from .50 to .42 by 2026-10-04 and leaves 1 claim untouched.* A world costs about 65 ms, a difference about 200 ms.

**Next:** stack **04**, as two parallel stacks — **04a** (browser: the join, then the map drawing itself) and **04b** (server: chapters + record 0015, the pipeline, the stream + replay, evals + ensemble + spread). Plan: `stack-04-generation.md`. **Kent answered every open question on 2026-09-17 — `plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md` — and the plan is rewritten to match. Nothing is waiting on him.**

---

## 3. Read these, in this order (about 50 minutes)

1. `AGENTS.md` — the rules of the repo and the working agreements. **Binding.**
2. `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — §1, §3 (eleven decisions — do not reopen them), §6.1–§6.2 (what generation must do), §7 (UX-1 to UX-14), §9 (fourteen invariants), §10 (anti-patterns), §12.
3. `ARCHITECTURE.md` — especially §2 (the model proposes; our code disposes) and §3 (the eight steps of a generation, with what is already built marked). **You must update it in the same pull request that makes a section real.**
4. `spec/README.md`, `spec/vocabulary.md`, then `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (the feedback-arrow rule and the refusal codes), `propagation.md` B4–B7, `diff.md` (including **open question 7**), and `spec/workbench/README.md` + `diff-view.md` (the `WorldSource` seam).
5. `docs/adr/README.md`, then records **0006** (the model boundary — the verified API specifics), **0008**, **0012** (replay mode), **0003**, **0014**.
6. **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-03-round-2.md`** — eleven decisions and fourteen small ones. Binding on every later stack. Then **`plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md`** — six decisions and eight small ones for stack 04.
7. `plans/stack-04-generation.md`.

---

## 4. How Kent works — the rules that will get your work rejected if you break them

**Build aggressively through milestones.** Kent's own words: *"build aggressively through milestones, I edit after the fact."* He is a co-developer, not an approver standing at a gate. Decision records and spec chapters still come first in the *stack order* — the bottom pull request of every stack is docs-only — but code above them proceeds while he reads. **How to ask him — this worked.** Collect the open questions; have a read-only Opus agent analyse them for *the most principled, simplest-to-maintain design, balanced against functionality*, sorting them into "needs Kent" and "falls out of something already decided"; then put the first group to him with the **question tool**: each in plain words with the Hormuz example, what changes on screen and in code, the recommended option first. **Write plainly.** No unexplained jargon, abbreviations, or symbols; each passage stands alone; short and punchy. When you cite an invariant such as INV-4, add a few words saying what it means.

## 5. Git and pull requests (decision record 0009)

- **Branch names:** `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` — `feat/04a-join`, `spec/04b-generation`.
- **Commit messages:** Conventional Commits — `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`, `chore:`, `ci:`, plus `spec:` and `adr:`. End agent-written commits with the co-author line your session instructions give you.
- **Stacks:** bottom pull request targets `main`; each above targets its parent — `gh pr create --base <parent-branch>`. **At most four deep** — which is why stack 04 is two stacks.
- **Pull request body, three headings:** *What* · *Which invariant it satisfies* · *What is deliberately not here*. End with the generated-with line your session instructions give you.
- **Never commit or push to `main` directly.**

### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is

When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.

### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)

**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:

```bash
gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
```

After a parent merges:

1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
   - *It is not a superset* (main moved for other reasons). `git rebase --onto origin/main <old-parent-tip> <branch>`, confirm `git diff --stat <reviewed-tip> HEAD -- <your dirs>` is empty, `git push --force-with-lease`, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.
3. **Run a join check before merging the second of two parallel stacks**: both test suites and the end-to-end test on the rebased top branch. In stack 03 it caught an end-to-end assertion that typed in a fixture number the other stack had changed.
4. **After changing a pull request's base by hand, GitHub can keep a stale `CONFLICTING` and schedule no checks at all** (stack 04, #39): confirm `gh pr view <n> --json mergeable` is `MERGEABLE` and that `gh pr checks <n>` lists jobs BEFORE waiting on them; if not, `gh pr close <n> && gh pr reopen <n>` makes it recompute and run CI. GitHub also did not restack a child whose branch had been force-pushed — use the `rebase --onto` route above and prove the tree is identical to the reviewed tip.
5. Afterwards: delete branches locally and with `gh api -X DELETE repos/kgang/katalyst/git/refs/heads/<branch>`, `git worktree remove` each worktree, `git fetch --prune`. Leave the `entire/*` branches alone — they are the checkpoint tool's.

## 7. The worktree pattern

Every sub-agent gets its own checkout of its own branch under **`../katalyst-wt/<branch-slug>/`**. The main checkout stays on `main` and is never used by a sub-agent.

- **One agent per worktree**, except chapter writers, who may share one **only** when their files are disjoint and **none of them runs a git command** — the coordinator commits for them.
- **Disjoint owned files**, listed in the brief. "Touch nothing outside it. If something outside it must change, write why in your report."
- **Agents never push, never open a pull request, never touch `main`.** The coordinator reviews, then pushes and opens the pull request.
- A resumed agent (send it a message) keeps its context — use that for fix rounds and for sweeps of files it wrote. You can point a resumed agent at a *different* worktree when the fix has to land on another branch.

## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

commit 54ea4eddc494034077a89bbf73020d7eb918e1b8
Author: Kent Gang <kent.y.gang@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 21 15:32:40 2026 +0300

    fix(canvas): a tile says where its ports are, so a wire is drawn before anything is measured
    
    **The root.** A wire is drawn between two ports — the sockets on a tile's
    edges — and the drawing library refuses to draw one whose ports it cannot
    place. Left to itself it places them by measuring the rendered tile, through
    the same `ResizeObserver` notification a busy browser abandons when too many
    fall due in one frame; an abandoned one is never delivered. #37 met that
    notification as tiles that never appeared and answered it by telling the
    library each tile's box outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half was
    left over, and the arrow stayed off the glass for the life of the page.
    
    **Measured three ways.** Drop every tile's notification and keep the glass's:
    seven tiles drawn, none hidden, twenty-eight ports on the glass, and not one
    arrow. Drop only the insurance premium's: the two arrows touching it go, and
    only those. Drop only the strait's: its three go. And in the wild, on ports
    nobody else on this machine held, with sixteen busy loops alongside — one run
    in two hundred at six workers lost `H->C` exactly that way, with every tile in
    place.
    
    **One rule, not two: a tile is told its box and where its ports sit, from the
    one place that worked them out.** `graph/ports.ts` is that place. It holds the
    four ports every tile has, their two shares of the tile's height, their size
    and their standoff, and the one piece of arithmetic that turns a height into
    four boxes. `toFlow` hands those boxes to the library beside `initialWidth`
    and `initialHeight`; `Tile.tsx` writes the very same numbers onto the elements
    it draws; `wires/plates.ts` reads the shares and the standoff from there
    instead of writing them down a third time. Nothing measures a port, nothing
    waits for a measurement, and nothing polls: `isNodeInitialized` accepts a
    declared port alongside a declared width, so both ends of every arrow are
    known on the first frame.
    
    **Declared and measured are the same numbers, and that matters.** The library
    keeps measuring, and `adoptUserNodes` rebuilds a node's port bounds from what
    was declared every time the map is redrawn — so a declared offset that
    disagreed with the measured one would jump a wire's ends back and forth on
    every hover. Driven through the installed library with the measurement
    simulated at the browser's own layout unit, one sixty-fourth of a pixel, the
    worst move is 0.0056 px. The ports render where they rendered before, to a
    hundredth of a pixel, and `socketsFor` returns the numbers it returned before,
    unchanged.
    
    **What this replaces.** A hook that asked the library to re-measure every tile
    eight times a second, on the state of `useNodesInitialized`. That flag is
    permanently false in this app — the canvas builds new node objects on every
    change, so the library's `measured` is discarded and, with neither default
    nodes nor an `onNodesChange`, never written back — so the asking never stopped
    and the fix worked only because it never stopped. The hook is gone.
    
    The end-to-end suite now checks every arrow by name on the stored example, not
    only the one an edit is made to; a map drawing six of eight was invisible to
    it. `test_the_arrows_are_drawn_when_the_browser_drops_a_size_notification`
    keeps its shim and now asserts the same eight, so it says *nothing changes*
    rather than *something was drawn*.

    test_a_port_is_placed_from_the_height_the_box_was_declared_at
    test_a_declared_port_is_where_the_tile_draws_it
    test_a_wire_attaches_where_the_plate_expects_it
    test_the_arrows_are_drawn_when_the_browser_drops_a_size_notification

1	/**
2	 * Turning a world into the tiles and wires the canvas draws.
3	 *
4	 * One function, no arithmetic, and nothing invented: every tile below stands
5	 * for a claim the server sent, every wire for an arrow the server sent, and the
6	 * only judgement made here is which tiles there is room to draw.
7	 */
8	
9	import type { Node } from "@xyflow/react";
10	import type { ClaimView, LinkMode, WorldView } from "../world";
11	import { NOT_ON_THIS_MAP } from "../world/naming";
12	import type { LayoutEdge, LayoutTile } from "./elkGraph";
13	import { TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, TILE_WIDTH, tileHeight } from "./geometry";
14	import { assignLayers, capLayers } from "./layers";
15	import type { CausalEdge } from "./wires/CausalWire";
16	
17	/** A tile standing for one claim. */
18	export type ClaimNode = Node<
19	  { claim: ClaimView; isHypothesis: boolean; versions?: number; height: number },
20	  "claim"
21	>;
22	
23	/** A tile standing for the claims a column had no room for. */
24	export type OverflowNode = Node<{ count: number }, "overflow">;
25	
26	/** A rectangle held open where a claim is about to arrive. Never a claim. */
27	export type SkeletonNode = Node<{ words: string }, "skeleton">;
28	
29	/** Everything the canvas draws as a box. */
30	export type MapNode = ClaimNode | OverflowNode | SkeletonNode;
31	
32	/**
33	 * One rectangle the map is holding open, reduced to what drawing one needs.
34	 *
35	 * Stated here rather than imported from the reducer that produces them, so that
36	 * the picture depends on no part of the machinery that reads a stream: this is
37	 * the whole of what the canvas needs to know about a thing that is not a claim.
38	 */
39	export interface ReservedBox {
40	  /** The rectangle's name. A box's name, never a claim's. */
41	  readonly id: string;
42	  /** The one line it carries. */
43	  readonly words: string;
44	  /** The open claim it hangs off, so the layout puts it one column further right. */
45	  readonly after: string | null;
46	}
47	
48	/**
49	 * A wire, carrying everything it needs to say its five things at once.
50	 *
51	 * How it is routed is filled in by the canvas rather than here: a wire that has
52	 * to skip a column needs to know where the other tiles ended up, and only the
53	 * canvas knows that.
54	 */
55	export type MapEdge = CausalEdge;
56	
57	/** What the canvas needs in order to draw a world. */
58	export interface MapDrawing {
59	  /** The tiles, without positions — those come from the layout. */
60	  readonly nodes: readonly MapNode[];
61	  /** The wires, as they will be drawn. */
62	  readonly edges: readonly MapEdge[];
63	  /**
64	   * Every tile with the height it will be drawn at, which is the height the
65	   * layout reserves for it. One number, worked out once, used by both.
66	   */
67	  readonly tiles: readonly LayoutTile[];
68	  /**
69	   * The arrows the layout gets a look at.
70	   *
71	   * Not the same list as the wires. Feedback arrows are left out, because a
72	   * left-to-right order cannot be worked out from a map with a loop in it, and
73	   * an arrow that stands in for collapsed tiles is put in, so the collapsed tile
74	   * lands in the column it belongs to.
75	   */
76	  readonly layoutEdges: readonly LayoutEdge[];
77	}
78	
79	/** Which socket a wire of this kind leaves from, and which it arrives at. */
80	function sockets(mode: LinkMode): { source: string; target: string } {
81	  return mode === "sustain"
82	    ? { source: "out-sustain", target: "in-sustain" }
83	    : { source: "out-trigger", target: "in-trigger" };
84	}
85	
86	/**
87	 * What the tile standing in for a column's collapsed claims is called.
88	 *
89	 * The canvas reads the column back out of it, so that activating one of those
90	 * tiles can open the outline filtered to that column — the claims behind it
91	 * already have items there, and the tile only has to point at them.
92	 */
93	export const OVERFLOW_PREFIX = "more-in-column-";
94	
95	/** The identifier of the tile standing in for a column's collapsed claims. */
96	function overflowId(layer: number): string {
97	  return `${OVERFLOW_PREFIX}${layer}`;
98	}
99	
100	/**
101	 * What every reserved rectangle's name starts with.
102	 *
103	 * It is how the canvas tells a box from a claim without asking the reducer:
104	 * nothing may be selected, focused or asked about under one of these names,
105	 * because there is nothing there yet.
106	 */
107	export const RESERVED_PREFIX = "skeleton:";
108	
109	/**
110	 * Work out the tiles, the wires, and what the layout gets to see.
111	 *
112	 * @param world The world as the source handed it over.
113	 * @param heights How tall each tile is to be drawn, when something outside knows
114	 *   better than this claim alone does. A diff draws two worlds in one coordinate
115	 *   space, and a claim can need more room in one of them than in the other — it
116	 *   grows badges when an edit touched it — so the box is reserved for the taller
117	 *   of the two and neither painting moves anything. Left out, each tile is as
118	 *   tall as its own content.
119	 * @param reserved The rectangles being held open at the growing edge of a map
120	 *   that is still being built. Empty on every finished map. Each one is drawn at
121	 *   a tile's floor height and is pulled into the column after the claim it hangs
122	 *   off by an arrow the layout sees and nobody draws — the same trick the tile
123	 *   standing in for a full column already uses.
124	 */
125	export function toFlow(
126	  world: WorldView,
127	  heights?: ReadonlyMap<string, number>,
128	  reserved: readonly ReservedBox[] = [],
129	): MapDrawing {
130	  const ids = world.claims.map((claim) => claim.id);
131	  const { shown, overflows } = capLayers(assignLayers(ids, world.links));
132	  const drawn = new Set(shown.map((one) => one.id));
133	  const byId = new Map(world.claims.map((claim) => [claim.id, claim]));
134	
135	  const nodes: MapNode[] = [];
136	  for (const placed of shown) {
137	    const claim = byId.get(placed.id);
138	    if (claim === undefined) {
139	      continue;
140	    }
141	    nodes.push({
142	      id: claim.id,
143	      type: "claim",
144	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
145	      draggable: false,
146	      data: {
147	        claim,
148	        isHypothesis: claim.id === world.hypothesisId,
149	        versions: world.versions,
150	        height: heights?.get(claim.id) ?? tileHeight(claim),
151	      },
152	    });
153	  }
154	  for (const overflow of overflows) {
155	    nodes.push({
156	      id: overflowId(overflow.layer),
157	      type: "overflow",
158	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
159	      draggable: false,
160	      data: { count: overflow.count },
161	    });
162	  }
163	
164	  // Only arrows between two tiles that are actually drawn become wires. An
165	  // arrow into a collapsed claim has nowhere to land, and the collapsed tile
166	  // says in words that those claims are still on the map.
167	  const claimWords = new Map(world.claims.map((claim) => [claim.id, claim.claim]));
168	  const edges: MapEdge[] = world.links
169	    .filter((link) => drawn.has(link.source) && drawn.has(link.target))
170	    .map((link) => {
171	      const { source, target } = sockets(link.mode);
172	      return {
173	        id: link.id,
174	        source: link.source,
175	        target: link.target,
176	        sourceHandle: source,
177	        targetHandle: target,
178	        // One kind of wire, drawn by us. How it gets from one end to the other
179	        // is worked out by the canvas, which is the only thing that knows where
180	        // the other tiles ended up.
181	        type: "causal" as const,
182	        // What a reader who never sees the picture hears instead. Everything
183	        // the stroke says, said in words.
184	        ariaLabel:
185	          `arrow from ${claimWords.get(link.source) ?? NOT_ON_THIS_MAP} ` +
186	          `to ${claimWords.get(link.target) ?? NOT_ON_THIS_MAP}`,
187	        data: {
188	          shape: link.shape,
189	          strength: link.strength,
190	          mode: link.mode,
191	          lag: link.lag,
192	          reflexive: link.reflexive,
193	          provenance: link.provenance,
194	          conditional: link.conditional,
195	        },
196	      };
197	    });
198	
199	  // What the layout sees. Feedback arrows are set aside: an arrow that points
200	  // backwards cannot help decide what comes first, and leaving it in would make
201	  // the map a loop with no beginning.
202	  const layoutEdges: LayoutEdge[] = world.links
203	    .filter((link) => !link.reflexive && drawn.has(link.source) && drawn.has(link.target))
204	    .map((link) => ({ id: link.id, source: link.source, target: link.target }));
205	
206	  // The collapsed tile is pulled into the right column by the same arrows that
207	  // would have reached the claims it stands for. These are never drawn.
208	  for (const overflow of overflows) {
209	    const hidden = new Set(overflow.hidden);
210	    const causes = new Set(
211	      world.links
212	        .filter((link) => !link.reflexive && hidden.has(link.target) && drawn.has(link.source))
213	        .map((link) => link.source),
214	    );
215	    for (const cause of causes) {
216	      layoutEdges.push({
217	        id: `standing-in:${cause}->${overflowId(overflow.layer)}`,
218	        source: cause,
219	        target: overflowId(overflow.layer),
220	      });
221	    }
222	  }
223	
224	  // The rectangles held open at the growing edge. They are boxes, not claims:
225	  // they never join `world.claims`, never reach the network, and carry nothing a
226	  // reader could mistake for a reading. Each is pulled into the column after the
227	  // claim it hangs off by an arrow the layout sees and nobody draws.
228	  for (const box of reserved) {
229	    nodes.push({
230	      id: box.id,
231	      type: "skeleton",
232	      position: { x: 0, y: 0 },
233	      draggable: false,
234	      // A rectangle is not a thing you can be on or ask about: it stands for a
235	      // claim that does not exist yet, and there is nothing to read out.
236	      selectable: false,
237	      focusable: false,
238	      data: { words: box.words },
239	    });
240	    if (box.after !== null && drawn.has(box.after)) {
241	      layoutEdges.push({
242	        id: `holding-open:${box.after}->${box.id}`,
243	        source: box.after,
244	        target: box.id,
245	      });
246	    }
247	  }
248	
249	  // **Every tile is told how big it is, and the layout and the drawing library
250	  // are told the same number.**
251	  //
252	  // A tile's box is not something to be discovered: it is 280 pixels wide
253	  // (`TILE_WIDTH`) and exactly as tall as the height this file worked out from
254	  // the claim, and the components draw themselves at precisely that size. The
255	  // layout engine has always been told. The drawing library was not — it was
256	  // left to measure each tile with a `ResizeObserver`, and **it draws nothing
257	  // it has not measured**: a node with no size is rendered `visibility:
258	  // hidden`.
259	  //
260	  // That is a promise the browser does not keep. When too many size
261	  // observations fall due in one frame the browser abandons the rest of them —
262	  // *"a ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications"* — and an
263	  // abandoned one is never delivered. A tile whose box then never changes size
264	  // again is never observed again, so it stays invisible for the life of the
265	  // page: the map holds its claims, in their places, and a reader cannot see
266	  // them. It is reachable today, on a cold machine, on the stored example.
267	  //
268	  // Saying the size is not a guess and not a duplicate: it is the one number,
269	  // handed to both of the things that need it, from the one place that worked
270	  // it out. The library still measures afterwards and still corrects itself —
271	  // `initialWidth` and `initialHeight` are what it asks for exactly so that a
272	  // caller who knows can say — and nothing downstream reads these back.
273	  //
274	  // **A reserved rectangle says how big it is too**, and it is the box that
275	  // needs saying most: it stands where a claim is about to arrive, so it is on
276	  // screen at the exact moment the page is busiest and the browser is likeliest
277	  // to drop an observation — and a rectangle nobody can see is a growing edge
278	  // that has stopped saying where the map is going.
279	  const tiles: LayoutTile[] = [];
280	  const sized = nodes.map((node) => {
281	    const height = node.type === "claim" ? node.data.height : TILE_MIN_HEIGHT;
282	    tiles.push({ id: node.id, height });
283	    return { ...node, initialWidth: TILE_WIDTH, initialHeight: height };
284	  }) as MapNode[];
285	
286	  return { nodes: sized, edges, layoutEdges, tiles };
287	}

commit 54ea4eddc494034077a89bbf73020d7eb918e1b8 Author: Kent Gang Date: Mon Sep 21 15:32:40 2026 +0300 fix(canvas): a tile says where its ports are, so a wire is drawn before anything is measured **The root.** A wire is drawn between two ports — the sockets on a tile's edges — and the drawing library refuses to draw one whose ports it cannot place. Left to itself it places them by measuring the rendered tile, through the same `ResizeObserver` notification a busy browser abandons when too many fall due in one frame; an abandoned one is never delivered. #37 met that notification as tiles that never appeared and answered it by telling the library each tile's box outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half was left over, and the arrow stayed off the glass for the life of the page. **Measured three ways.** Drop every tile's notification and keep the glass's: seven tiles drawn, none hidden, twenty-eight ports on the glass, and not one arrow. Drop only the insurance premium's: the two arrows touching it go, and only those. Drop only the strait's: its three go. And in the wild, on ports nobody else on this machine held, with sixteen busy loops alongside — one run in two hundred at six workers lost `H->C` exactly that way, with every tile in place. **One rule, not two: a tile is told its box and where its ports sit, from the one place that worked them out.** `graph/ports.ts` is that place. It holds the four ports every tile has, their two shares of the tile's height, their size and their standoff, and the one piece of arithmetic that turns a height into four boxes. `toFlow` hands those boxes to the library beside `initialWidth` and `initialHeight`; `Tile.tsx` writes the very same numbers onto the elements it draws; `wires/plates.ts` reads the shares and the standoff from there instead of writing them down a third time. Nothing measures a port, nothing waits for a measurement, and nothing polls: `isNodeInitialized` accepts a declared port alongside a declared width, so both ends of every arrow are known on the first frame. **Declared and measured are the same numbers, and that matters.** The library keeps measuring, and `adoptUserNodes` rebuilds a node's port bounds from what was declared every time the map is redrawn — so a declared offset that disagreed with the measured one would jump a wire's ends back and forth on every hover. Driven through the installed library with the measurement simulated at the browser's own layout unit, one sixty-fourth of a pixel, the worst move is 0.0056 px. commit 6bc90d33fc5b497933649bbaca757f3d4bfdef9f
Author: Kent Gang <kent.y.gang@gmail.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 21 15:32:40 2026 +0300

    fix(canvas): a tile the library never measured has no arrows drawn to it
    
    **The root.** A wire is drawn between two handles, and where a handle sits
    inside a tile is something the drawing library measures — through the same
    `ResizeObserver` notification a busy browser abandons when too many fall due in
    one frame. #37 met that as tiles that never appeared and fixed it by telling
    the library each tile's box outright; a box is not a handle, so the wire half
    was left. An abandoned notification is never delivered, so the arrow stays off
    the glass for the life of the page.
    
    **Measured three ways.** Drop every tile's notification and keep the glass's:
    seven tiles drawn, none hidden, twenty-eight handles on the glass, and not one
    arrow. Drop only the insurance premium's: the two arrows touching it go, and
    only those. Drop only the strait's: its three go. And in the wild, on ports
    nobody else on this machine held, with the fix reverted and sixteen busy loops
    alongside — one run in two hundred at six workers lost `H->C` exactly that way,
    with every tile in place.
    
    `useHandlesTheLibraryHasMeasured` asks the library to measure again and keeps
    asking until it says it has. `nodesInitialized` is that fact — false until every
    tile has handle bounds — so this acts on the state of the map rather than on a
    guess about timing, and asking is a direct measurement rather than another
    notification to be dropped. It is a timer rather than an animation frame
    because a browser produces no frames while nothing is changing, and nothing
    changing is precisely the fault; #37 learnt that one the hard way.
    
    The end-to-end helper no longer waits a missing arrow out. It asserts the arrow
    is there and names it, so a return of this fails in fifteen seconds instead of
    forty-five.
    
    test_the_arrows_are_drawn_when_the_browser_drops_a_size_notification
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Entire-Checkpoint: 01M32101EQEB5PE4BTK5V7E98E

- * **Nothing here reads a value the page has not settled on.** This test drives
- * two servers, a background layout thread and a drawing library that measures
- * its own boxes, so at any moment the screen may be showing the answer to the
- * question before last. Every read goes through one of the helpers below, and
- * each of them waits for a *named* signal rather than for a number of

- * for a whole new world and a whole new difference, and until they come back

3	/**
4	 * Waiting, and why every read in a browser test goes through it.
5	 *
6	 * **Nothing here reads a value the page has not settled on.** These tests drive
7	 * two servers, a background layout thread and a drawing library that measures
8	 * its own boxes, so at any moment the screen may be showing the answer to the
9	 * question before last. Every read goes through one of the helpers below, and
10	 * each of them waits for a *named* signal rather than for a number of
11	 * milliseconds — a sleep is a guess, and the build machine is about two and a
12	 * half times slower than the machine it was guessed on.
13	 *
14	 * They live in a file of their own because both browser tests need them, and a
15	 * helper copied into a second file is a second helper: the day one of these
16	 * learns about a new way the screen can lie, only one test would learn it.
17	 */
18	
19	/**
20	 * Wait until the map has been laid out, with every tile in a place of its own.
21	 *
22	 * Where the tiles go is worked out on a background thread, so for a moment after
23	 * the map appears the tiles are still stacked. Waiting for **every** tile to be
24	 * somewhere different is the honest signal, and it is the one that survives a
25	 * second layout: after a branch opens the tiles are already spread out from the
26	 * layout before it, so "more than one place" is satisfied before the new answer
27	 * has landed and says nothing at all.
28	 *
29	 * @param page The page the map is on.
30	 * @param tiles How many tiles this map has. A layered layout gives every tile a
31	 *   place of its own — two tiles on one spot is the collision the layout exists
32	 *   to prevent — so the count of places is the count of tiles exactly when the
33	 *   layout has landed.
34	 */
35	export async function waitForTheLayout(page: Page, tiles: number): Promise<void> {
36	  await expect(page.locator(".react-flow__node")).toHaveCount(tiles);
37	  await expect
38	    .poll(
39	      () =>
40	        page
41	          .locator(".react-flow__node")
42	          .evaluateAll(
43	            (nodes) => new Set(nodes.map((node) => (node as HTMLElement).style.transform)).size,
44	          ),
45	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the map was never laid out" },
46	    )
47	    .toBe(tiles);
48	  await expect(page.locator(".react-flow__node").first()).toBeVisible();
49	}

51	/**
52	 * Read one value off the screen, once the screen has settled on it.
53	 *
54	 * The shape is not decoration: it is what "settled" means here. A chip holds an
55	 * absence, then a number; waiting for the number's shape is waiting for the
56	 * engine. And the read itself is `textContent` rather than `innerText`, which
57	 * is empty until the drawing library has measured the tile.
58	 *
59	 * @param where The one element the value is in.
60	 * @param shape What the value looks like once it is there.
61	 */
62	export async function readWhenReady(where: Locator, shape: RegExp): Promise<string> {
63	  await expect(where).toBeVisible();
64	  await expect(where).toHaveText(shape);
65	  return ((await where.textContent()) ?? "").trim();
66	}

68	/**
69	 * Wait until the engine has answered for this branch and the map has been laid
70	 * out again.
71	 *
72	 * The line under the map names the branch it folded on, and it is written from
73	 * the world the engine handed back — so it is there exactly when that world is.
74	 *
75	 * @param page The page the map is on.
76	 * @param branch The branch's name, as the reader typed it.
77	 * @param tiles How many tiles the map has with this branch folded on.
78	 */
79	export async function waitForTheBranch(page: Page, branch: string, tiles: number): Promise<void> {
80	  await expect(page.locator(".map-bar__where")).toContainText(branch);
81	  await expect(page.locator(".map-origin")).toContainText(`the branch "${branch}" folded onto it`);
82	  await waitForTheLayout(page, tiles);
83	}

85	/**
86	 * Wait until the map has said, out loud, what this edit did.
87	 *
88	 * This is the signal an edit is finished. The counts in the sentence are the
89	 * engine's own, one per claim it called shifted, so the sentence cannot be there
90	 * until the difference is — and it is a *different* sentence from the one before
91	 * the edit, which is what makes waiting for it waiting rather than passing.
92	 *
93	 * @param page The page the map is on.
94	 * @param sentence The whole line, word for word.
95	 */
96	export async function waitForTheAnswer(page: Page, sentence: string): Promise<void> {
97	  await expect(page.locator(".map-live")).toHaveText(sentence);
98	}

100	/**
101	 * Wait until the map has stopped moving, and say where it came to rest.
102	 *
103	 * Framing the map is an animation, so the transform is read twice and believed
104	 * only when the two agree. What it is for is the claim that flipping between the
105	 * two worlds moves nothing: a transform read mid-frame would make that claim
106	 * about two different moments.
107	 */
108	export async function whereTheMapCameToRest(page: Page): Promise<string> {
109	  const viewport = page.locator(".react-flow__viewport");
110	  let last = "";
111	  await expect
112	    .poll(
113	      async () => {
114	        const now = (await viewport.getAttribute("style")) ?? "";
115	        const settled = now !== "" && now === last;
116	        last = now;
117	        return settled;
118	      },
119	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the map never stopped moving" },
120	    )
121	    .toBe(true);
122	  return last;
123	}

125	/** Which claim the keyboard is standing on, or nothing when it is off the map. */
126	export function standingOn(page: Page): Promise<string | undefined> {
127	  return page.evaluate(
128	    () => document.activeElement?.closest<HTMLElement>(".react-flow__node")?.dataset.id,
129	  );
130	}

132	/**
133	 * Put the keyboard on one claim's tile, the way a reader would, and wait until
134	 * it is there.
135	 *
136	 * **A map key only works when the keyboard is on the map**, and that is the
137	 * product's rule rather than this test's convenience: Space belongs to whatever
138	 * button the keyboard is on, so `useMapKeys` hands it over when there is one and
139	 * flips the two worlds only when there is not. Where focus happens to be after
140	 * a command has run is not something a test may assume — under load it is
141	 * sometimes a button, and then the keystroke is correctly ignored and the test
142	 * fails for a reason that is not a fault.
143	 *
144	 * @param page The page the map is on.
145	 * @param claim The claim whose tile the keyboard should stand on.
146	 */
147	export async function standOn(page: Page, claim: string): Promise<void> {
148	  await expect
149	    .poll(
150	      async () => {
151	        // The focusing is inside the poll, not before it. A re-render replaces
152	        // the tile's element and the keyboard falls back to the page, so asking
153	        // again and again whether it landed would ask for ever; what has to be
154	        // retried is the standing, not the looking.
155	        await page.locator(`.react-flow__node[data-id="${claim}"]`).focus();
156	        return await standingOn(page);
157	      },
158	      { timeout: 15_000, message: `the keyboard never stood on ${claim}` },
159	    )
160	    .toBe(claim);
161	}
162	
163	/**
164	 * Where one tile sits, once the drawing library has put it somewhere.
165	 *
166	 * **The place, and nothing else about the element.** The library writes several
167	 * things into a tile's style — its stacking order, whether the pointer may reach
168	 * it, and whether it is visible at all, which it turns off and on again as it
169	 * measures boxes — and only one of them is where the tile is. Comparing the
170	 * whole style across a change compares those too, and then "nothing already
171	 * placed moved" fails on a tile that was merely being re-measured. For the same
172	 * reason this waits for the tile to have a **place** rather than for it to be
173	 * visible: where it sits is a fact about the layout, and whether it is painted
174	 * this instant is not.
175	 *
176	 * @param tile The tile's element on the map.
177	 */
178	export async function whereTheTileSits(tile: Locator): Promise<string> {
179	  await expect(tile).toHaveCount(1);
180	  await expect
181	    .poll(
182	      async () => /translate\([^)]*\)/.exec((await tile.getAttribute("style")) ?? "")?.[0] ?? "",
183	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the tile was never placed" },
184	    )
185	    .not.toBe("");
186	  return /translate\([^)]*\)/.exec((await tile.getAttribute("style")) ?? "")?.[0] ?? "";
187	}

1	/**
2	 * Where a tile's ports are, and the one place that says so.
3	 *
4	 * A **port** is the socket a wire attaches to. Every tile has four: a pair on
5	 * the left edge for arrows arriving and a pair on the right for arrows leaving,
6	 * and in each pair the upper socket is for an arrow that fires once and stays
7	 * fired, the lower for one that only holds while its cause holds. What a wire
8	 * means is visible at the socket before you follow it anywhere.
9	 *
10	 * **A port's place is declared, not discovered — and that is the whole point of
11	 * this file.** The drawing library draws a wire between two ports, and left to
12	 * itself it finds out where a port is by measuring the page, through the very
13	 * same browser notification a busy browser drops. A wire whose ends were never
14	 * measured is not drawn at all: the map holds every claim, in its place, and
15	 * says nothing about how they are joined, which is the wrong picture of the
16	 * argument and a silent one. #37 met the same dropped notification as tiles
17	 * that never appeared and answered it by telling the library each tile's box
18	 * outright. A box is not a port, so the wire half of it was left over. This is
19	 * the rest of the same answer: told its box *and* where its ports sit, a tile
20	 * can have its wires drawn on the first frame with nothing measured at all.
21	 *
22	 * So every number a port has is written here, and written **once**. The tile
23	 * puts these numbers straight onto the element it draws; the drawing library is
24	 * handed the same numbers; `wires/plates.ts` places a plate against them. This
25	 * file must never read a port's place back off the screen, and nothing else may
26	 * write one down a second time — two places that have to agree are two places
27	 * that one day will not.
28	 */

30	import type { NodeHandle } from "@xyflow/react";
31	import { Position } from "@xyflow/react";
32	import type { LinkMode } from "../world";
33	import { TILE_WIDTH } from "./geometry";
34	
35	/**
36	 * How wide a port is, in pixels — two steps of the eight-pixel grid the whole
37	 * interface sits on.
38	 *
39	 * It straddles the tile's edge, half of it inside and half outside, which is
40	 * why it is exactly twice the standoff below.
41	 */
42	export const PORT_WIDTH = 16;
43	
44	/** How tall a port is, in pixels: enough for one bar, a gap and a second bar. */
45	export const PORT_HEIGHT = 6;
46	
47	/**
48	 * How far past the tile's edge a wire attaches, in pixels.
49	 *
50	 * A wire that met the tile flush would have its last few pixels drawn under the
51	 * tile's own outline. Eight pixels clear is one step of the grid.
52	 */
53	export const PORT_STANDOFF = 8;
54	
55	/**
56	 * How far down a tile each of the two sockets sits, as a share of its height.
57	 *
58	 * A share rather than a number of pixels, because a tile is as tall as its own
59	 * content: the pair has to stay evenly spaced about the middle on a tile of any
60	 * height. Read by `wires/plates.ts` as well, which has to know where a wire
61	 * will start before a single wire has been drawn.
62	 */
63	export const DOWN_THE_TILE: Readonly<Record<LinkMode, number>> = {
64	  trigger: 0.38,
65	  sustain: 0.62,
66	};
67	
68	/** What a port is called. These four names are what a wire names its ends by. */
69	export type PortId = "in-trigger" | "in-sustain" | "out-trigger" | "out-sustain";
70	
71	/** One socket on the edge of a tile. */
72	export interface Port {
73	  /** Its name, which is what a wire asks for. */
74	  readonly id: PortId;
75	  /** Whether wires leave from it or arrive at it. */
76	  readonly kind: "source" | "target";
77	  /** Which edge of the tile it is on. */
78	  readonly edge: Position;
79	  /** Which kind of push attaches here. Also what the socket is drawn as. */
80	  readonly mode: LinkMode;
81	}
82	
83	/**
84	 * The four ports every tile has, in the order they are drawn.
85	 *
86	 * Arriving before leaving, and within each pair the one that fires once before
87	 * the one that holds — the same top-to-bottom order the sockets are drawn in,
88	 * so the list reads the way the tile looks.
89	 */
90	export const PORTS: readonly Port[] = [
91	  { id: "in-trigger", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "trigger" },
92	  { id: "in-sustain", kind: "target", edge: Position.Left, mode: "sustain" },
93	  { id: "out-trigger", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "trigger" },
94	  { id: "out-sustain", kind: "source", edge: Position.Right, mode: "sustain" },
95	];
96	
97	/** A port's box, in the tile's own coordinates, with the tile's corner at zero. */
98	export interface PortBox {
99	  /** Its left edge. Negative on the left of a tile: the port straddles the edge. */
100	  readonly x: number;
101	  /** Its top edge. */
102	  readonly y: number;
103	  /** How wide it is. */
104	  readonly width: number;
105	  /** How tall it is. */
106	  readonly height: number;
107	}
108	
109	/**
110	 * Where this port sits on a tile of this height.
111	 *
112	 * The one piece of arithmetic in this file, and every other number here and in
113	 * the tile comes out of it. The box straddles the tile's edge so that the wire
114	 * attaches a clear eight pixels outside it, and it is centred on the share of
115	 * the height the socket sits at.
116	 *
117	 * @param height How tall the tile is — the same number the layout reserved for
118	 *   it and the same number the tile is drawn at. A tile that grew a line
119	 *   because an edit touched it moves its ports down with it, and this is where
120	 *   that happens.
121	 * @param port Which of the four.
122	 */
123	export function portBox(height: number, port: Port): PortBox {
124	  return {
125	    x: port.edge === Position.Left ? -PORT_STANDOFF : TILE_WIDTH + PORT_STANDOFF - PORT_WIDTH,
126	    y: height * DOWN_THE_TILE[port.mode] - PORT_HEIGHT / 2,
127	    width: PORT_WIDTH,
128	    height: PORT_HEIGHT,
129	  };
130	}
131	
132	/**
133	 * Every port of a tile this tall, in the shape the drawing library takes them.
134	 *
135	 * Handed over with the tile's box, so that the library knows where both ends of
136	 * every wire are before it has measured anything. It keeps measuring afterwards
137	 * and rebuilds these from what it measures; the numbers are the same numbers,
138	 * because the tile was drawn from them.
139	 *
140	 * @param height How tall the tile is.
141	 */
142	export function portsOf(height: number): NodeHandle[] {
143	  return PORTS.map((port) => ({
144	    id: port.id,
145	    type: port.kind,
146	    position: port.edge,
147	    ...portBox(height, port),
148	  }));
149	}

151	/**
152	 * Which port a wire of this kind leaves from, and which it arrives at.
153	 *
154	 * @param mode Whether the push fires once or has to keep holding.
155	 */
156	export function portsForAWire(mode: LinkMode): {
157	  readonly source: PortId;
158	  readonly target: PortId;
159	} {
160	  return mode === "sustain"
161	    ? { source: "out-sustain", target: "in-sustain" }
162	    : { source: "out-trigger", target: "in-trigger" };
163	}

+ * arrows between them is the wrong picture of the argument, and a silent one —

+ * same fault arriving quieter.

+ * @param page The page the map is on.

+  const eight = ["B->M1", "B->M2", "B->R", "C->B", "H->B", "H->C", "H->N1", "R->B"];

+    .poll(() =>
+      page
+        .locator(".react-flow__edge")
+        .evaluateAll((wires) => wires.map((wire) => (wire as HTMLElement).dataset.id).sort()),
+    )
+    .toEqual(eight);
+}

  *
@@ -143,10 +170,11 @@ async function openThePanelOnTheArrow(page: Page, id: string): Promise<void> {

   await expect(page.locator(".map-origin")).toContainText("versions of the map");

chore(e2e): drop four throwaway configs that were committed by accident

`frontend/.tmp-e2e/` held four Playwright setting files written while one
browser failure was being chased — `pw-gen`, `pw-mine`, `pw-norec` and
`pw-replay`. Each was meant to live for an afternoon; three `git add -A`
commits swept them in instead.

They are worse than clutter. Every one of them names this machine's own
directories, two of them point at a scratch directory that no longer exists,
and `pw-replay` attaches to whatever is already listening on one hardcoded
port — which is the exact habit lesson 18 was written about: one worktree's
browser run quietly testing another branch's app. The project has one browser
setting file, `frontend/playwright.config.ts`, and it takes its ports from the
environment.

Nothing refers to them: the directory is deleted and `.gitignore` now keeps
the next one out.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git log --oneline -2
